name: Sam Loyd
knownFor: America's most famous puzzle-maker — and its most famous puzzle-hustler.
bio: Samuel Loyd was born in Philadelphia and raised in New York City. He was a strong chess player and a prolific, witty composer of chess problems, and he turned the same cleverness to puzzles of every kind, which he sold to newspapers and magazines and to the public.

He was a showman. Loyd claimed to have invented the fifteen-piece sliding puzzle that swept the country in the 1880s; the actual inventor was Noyes Chapman, who applied for a patent in 1880. His son published his collected puzzles after his death, and the historians of the field still sort fact from Loyd's own publicity.

events.text: Published a chess problem on a siege that had taken place in 1713, one of the many he wrote around a story.
Played in the Paris chess tournament, with little success.
Patented the rotary vanishing puzzles, including Get Off the Earth, Teddy and the Lion and The Disappearing Bicyclist.
The Strand Magazine called him "the prince of puzzlers".
Died on 10 April; his Cyclopedia of 5000 Puzzles appeared three years later.
Inducted into the US Chess Hall of Fame.

relevance: Loyd is widely named America's greatest puzzler and popularizer; Martin Gardner called him exactly that in 1957. He is also the textbook example of why puzzle history needs care, since Gardner went on to call him "obviously a hustler".
influence: He made the puzzle a popular entertainment, and for a time collaborated with Henry Dudeney. His 5000 Puzzles is still reprinted and is in the public domain.
